capabilities.target: CI runner container shell, with full workspace and environment access
GitHub branch push / PR open, using a PAT scoped to all org repositories
.agent/config.yaml: the agent's own model, tool list, autonomy, and network settings
Slack channel via a planned MCP integration

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body, public repo
Repository file contents read while reproducing and fixing the issue
Slack messages via a planned Slack MCP server (not yet connected)

instructions.note: Agent is told to pick up any issue labeled 'bug' and fix it end to end, with no scoping on which repos, how large a change may be, or when to stop.

The only defense against destructive commands or secret exfiltration is a plain-text prompt instruction, with no structural enforcement, while the agent holds broad shell, filesystem, and credential access.

Line 2 requires the agent to run whatever commands are needed to reproduce a bug, which routinely means following reproduction steps written inside the issue body, while line 5 tells it to ignore instructions that appear inside issues. The core workflow and the injection defense are in direct tension.

The agent is explicitly authorized to edit its own .agent/config.yaml 'if you need extra tools to finish a task', with no restriction on who or what may establish that need. This sanctions self-modification as a normal part of the workflow.

elements.name: GitHub organization (all repositories reachable via the org-wide PAT)

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding destructive or exfiltration commands
controls.decay_rationale: Enforcement depends entirely on the model choosing to comply. A more capable or adversarially-prompted model can rationalize, obfuscate, or split a prohibited action into steps that individually look benign (e.g., base64-encoding a token, or using git itself rather than an explicit 'delete' or 'exfiltrate' command).

controls.name: Prompt instruction to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Pure prompt-level defense against indirect injection. It is already undermined by the core workflow, which requires the model to read and act on reproduction steps written inside the untrusted issue body (prompt.md:2), and it decays further under model upgrades and longer task horizons.

controls.name: Container isolation on the CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: Limits host-level compromise and some lateral movement, but does not restrict network egress (network: unrestricted) or scope the credential available inside the container (ORG_WIDE_PAT in env), so it does not narrow exfiltration or lateral-repo-write paths. It is also a shared runner, which weakens isolation guarantees against co-located workloads.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist
controls.decay_rationale: An allowlist restricted to required destinations would sever exfiltration via shell network calls to attacker-controlled endpoints, independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Repository-scoped, minimally-privileged GitHub token
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped to only the single repository being worked on, with no workflow scope and no org-wide reach, would make cross-repo writes and workflow-trigger abuse structurally impossible regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Read-only or human-approved .agent/config.yaml
controls.decay_rationale: Mounting the config read-only, or gating writes behind a human-reviewed deployment step, removes the agent's ability to self-modify its own tools, model, or autonomy settings, independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Human approval before branch push / PR open
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate requires a human to see the actual diff and destination repository before changes leave the sandbox, independent of model behavior.

controls.name: Bounded step count and runtime
controls.decay_rationale: A finite max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes caps resource consumption and blast radius per task, independent of model behavior, narrowing (not fully severing) runaway-loop and cost/DoS risk.

controls.name: Audit logging of agent actions
controls.decay_rationale: No logging or audit trail is declared for shell commands, file writes, or pushes. Without one, compromise is not detectable after the fact and actions are not attributable to the triggering issue.

controls.name: Input injection classifier on issue content
controls.decay_rationale: A separate classifier screening issue bodies for embedded instructions would reduce, but not eliminate, the injection surface; it would still degrade under novel encodings and multi-turn payloads.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue content drives shell commands that can read and exfiltrate the org-wide PAT over unrestricted network egress

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue and add the 'bug' label via the issue template.

prompt.md:2 instructs the agent to run whatever commands it needs; the shell environment carries ORG_WIDE_PAT and has unrestricted network, so a command can read the token and send it to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: model: latest means the effective model is unpinned and can change without review; any observed model version change, or tasks running with much longer context/turns, should trigger reassessment.

evidence.observation: network: unrestricted and GITHUB_TOKEN (${ORG_WIDE_PAT}, repo+workflow scope on all org repos) are both present in the shell's environment.
Agent is told to run whatever commands it needs to reproduce and test, with no technical restriction on command choice or destination.
Any GitHub user can open an issue and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making issue content attacker-reachable.

recommendations.action: Add a network egress allowlist restricting outbound shell traffic to required destinations (package registries, GitHub API); block arbitrary outbound HTTP.
Scope the GitHub token to the single target repository with minimum permissions and inject it only into the push step, not the general shell environment.

findings.title: Injected execution (TC2): mandated 'reproduce and test' workflow hands shell execution to untrusted issue content

attack_path.note: prompt.md:2 instructs the agent to run whatever commands are needed to reproduce the issue; a malicious 'reproduction step' embedded in the issue is executed as part of normal operation.

forecast.watch_signal: Unpinned model string changing; removal or softening of prompt.md:5; max_steps being raised without a corresponding command allowlist being added.

evidence.observation: 'Run whatever commands you need to reproduce and test' gives the model open-ended command authority as the normal, expected workflow.
The instruction to ignore instructions inside issues directly conflicts with needing to follow issue-provided reproduction steps, weakening this defense for this exact path.

recommendations.action: Run reproduction/test commands inside a locked-down, network-isolated sandbox with a command allowlist, instead of relying solely on prompt instruction.

findings.title: Self modification (TC3): instruction-sanctioned editing of .agent/config.yaml allows untrusted content to persist a compromise across sessions

attack_path.note: prompt.md:6 explicitly authorizes the agent to edit .agent/config.yaml 'if you need extra tools'; an injected instruction can be framed as a legitimate tooling need.

forecast.watch_signal: Any diff to .agent/config.yaml that is not accompanied by a corresponding, separately reviewed change in version control; model string left unpinned.

evidence.observation: 'You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task' authorizes self-modification with no restriction on where the perceived need originates.
model, tools, autonomy, and network settings all live in a file the agent can write via fs.write, and persist into every future run.

recommendations.action: Mount .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent process, or require a separate human-reviewed deployment step for any change to tools, model, autonomy, or network settings.
Remove prompt.md:6; the agent should never be instructed that it may expand its own tool access.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): an org-wide PAT exposed to shell lets a repo-level fixer agent write to any repository in the organization

attack_path.note: GITHUB_TOKEN is a raw environment variable available to the shell, usable directly via git/gh CLI independent of any scoping github.push_branch itself might apply.
Token carries repo+workflow scope on all org repositories, not just the one this agent is meant to fix issues in.

forecast.watch_signal: PAT scope widened further, or additional org repos/workflows added without re-scoping the token.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos, far broader than the single repository the agent is meant to work in.
shell.run is listed alongside the same environment, so the raw token can be used directly via CLI commands.

recommendations.action: Issue a repo-scoped fine-grained PAT or GitHub App installation token limited to the one repository, instead of an org-wide PAT with workflow scope.
Add a human approval gate with raw-action review, showing the actual diff and destination repository, before any branch push or PR open.

findings.title: Unbounded autonomy on shared infrastructure: no step or runtime limit enables resource exhaustion and cross-tenant impact

attack_path.note: Could prompt or induce a long or looping reproduction/fix attempt.
max_steps: null and no max_runtime_minutes declared anywhere.
Runs on a shared CI runner alongside other tenants' workloads.

forecast.watch_signal: Median task runtime or step count trending upward with no step/runtime limit added; incidents of CI runner contention or billing spikes.

evidence.observation: max_steps: null, and no max_runtime_minutes is declared anywhere, so a task has no upper bound on steps or wall-clock time.
Agent runs on a shared CI runner with other tenants, so unbounded resource consumption can affect workloads beyond this agent's own task.

recommendations.action: Set a finite max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes, and a per-task compute/cost budget.
Add logging/audit trail of all shell commands, file writes, and pushes, attributable to the triggering issue.

findings.title: Forecast: planned Slack MCP server would reopen a lethal-trifecta-style path through a new untrusted channel

forecast.watch_signal: Addition of a Slack MCP server entry to the client config, or any new MCP client config diff.

evidence.observation: Team plans to add a Slack MCP server next quarter; no scoping, authentication, or definition-pinning details are specified yet.

recommendations.action: Before connecting the Slack MCP server, require signed/pinned tool definitions, authenticate the server, and treat all inbound Slack content as untrusted input subject to the same containment controls recommended for issue content.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because every identified path runs from untrusted, publicly-reachable GitHub issue content (any user can open an issue and apply the 'bug' label) to S3-class sinks: shell execution with a broad, org-wide credential and unrestricted network egress; self-editable agent configuration; and branch pushes scoped across the entire organization. Residual risk stays critical because one finding (f.unbounded_autonomy_dos) has no applicable control at all -- there is no step limit, runtime limit, or audit trail -- so its residual equals its inherent risk. The other four present findings drop from critical to high on the strength of two prompt-level instructions (ctl.instr_no_delete_exfil, ctl.instr_ignore_injected), which are dependent, behavioral controls; the declared container sandbox (ctl.container_sandbox) was not credited against these specific paths because it explicitly does not restrict network egress or credential scope, which is what each of these paths exploits. Because the model is configured as 'latest' (unpinned, swappable: true), the model_upgrade trigger that defeats these dependent controls is effectively already live rather than a future condition, which is why forecast risk is also critical with no further triggering event required. The single highest-leverage fix is removing the self-config permission (prompt.md:6) and locking .agent/config.yaml, followed by replacing the org-wide PAT with a repository-scoped token and adding a network egress allowlist; these are the only controls in this design capable of severing rather than merely narrowing a path.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the runtime notes provided; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior, logs, or a live penetration test of the agent.

No MCP or A2A protocol configuration was provided for the current tool set (shell.run, fs.write, fs.read, github.push_branch, github.open_pr); these are treated as directly-invoked tools rather than protocol-mediated connections. If any are in fact served via an MCP server, protocol-level checks (auth method, definition pinning, peer identity) have not been evaluated and could change the rating.

fs.read is listed as an available tool in .agent/config.yaml but has no assigned stable id in the case material; its risk is folded into the general trust analysis of in.repo_files and in.issue_body rather than modeled as its own capability.

The planned Slack MCP server (elem.slack_mcp_planned) is not yet built; the associated forecast finding, planned capability, and planned input are necessarily speculative and should be reassessed in detail once an actual MCP configuration exists.

Whether the container sandbox restricts anything beyond host-level filesystem isolation (seccomp profile, capability dropping, etc.) is not described in the artifacts; it is scored conservatively as not narrowing the network-egress or credential-exposure paths.
